content: The pascal (symbol: Pa) is the SI-derived unit used to measure pressure or stress, including Young's modulus and tensile strength. It is defined as one newton per square meter or equivalently one joule per cubic meter. In everyday life, the pascal is most commonly recognized in meteorological air-pressure reports, where it is often expressed in kilopascals (1 kPa = 1000 Pa). The kilopascal is also widely used in other contexts, such as on bicycle tire labels. One kilopascal is approximately 1% of atmospheric pressure at sea level, and one hectopascal is equivalent to one millibar. The unit is named after Blaise Pascal, a renowned French mathematician, physicist, and philosopher known for his experiments with barometers, which measure air pressure. The name pascal was officially adopted for the SI unit of pressure (newton per square meter) by the 14th General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) in 1971. The conversion of 25 millibars to 760 torr is also used in various industries, including pneumatic fluid power (ISO R554), aerospace (ISO 2533), and petroleum (ISO 5024). In 1985, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) recommended standardizing atmospheric pressure to 100,000 Pa, which is equivalent to 1 bar or 750 torr. This definition is also applied in the compressor and pneumatic tool industries (ISO 2787). The Unicode character set includes dedicated symbols for the pascal (Pa) and kilopascal (kPa), but these are deprecated and exist only for backward compatibility with older character sets. Meteorologists have historically measured atmospheric pressure in millibars. After the introduction of SI units, many preferred to retain the familiar pressure values, leading to the use of hectopascals (hPa) for air pressure measurements. Hectopascals are equivalent to millibars, but in most other fields, pressure is expressed in kilopascals, as the hecto prefix is rarely used outside meteorology. In Canada, following official metrication, meteorologists now use kilopascals (kPa) for weather reports, as seen in sources like CTV News and CBC Weather. However, in some other countries, hectopascals remain in use, as evidenced by organizations like KNMI, KMI, DWD, JMA, MDD, and NOAA. In older measurement systems, the unit of pressure in the mts system was the pièze (symbol: pz), which is equivalent to one kilopascal. In the cgs system, the unit of pressure was the barye (symbol: Ba), which is equal to one decipascal. Modern vehicle owner manuals now specify tire inflation pressures in kilopascals.
